pages.text: A tumour is not one enemy but a population of competing clones, each with its own mutations and its own fitness f_i. A clone gains share only when it beats the average: dx_i/dt = x_i(f_i − Σx_j f_j). Every treatment changes the fitnesses - and so it selects whichever clones it happens not to kill.

That is how $(thing)drug resistance$() arises: a resistant cell one in a thousand, with an advantage of s = 0.5 per day under treatment, is 96% of the tumour twenty days later. It was there before the drug - the drug only chose it. Hence combination therapy: a clone resistant to two independent drugs at once is rarer by the product of their odds.
In the $(item)Evolution Engine$(), metastatic spores, an immortal line and an enzyme under selection leave a $(item)Resistant Clone Colony$().
The cells that survived the last treatment - and so the ones that make the next tumour. Selection, not malice.$(br2)Made in $(item)Evolution Engine$().
